7778.t: BM6235: Transport Processes in Biological System
7778.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM6235 : Transport Processes in Biological System { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics in Biological Systems: Introduction to Fluid Mechanics: Properties of fluids and Viscosity. Basic Fluid Dynamics: Continuity equation, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and Application of Bernoulli’s equation. Advanced Fluid Dynamics: Navier-Stokes equations and Hagen-Poiseuille equation.
Module 2: Physiological Fluid Dynamics: Physiological Properties of Biological Fluids: Fluid flow in the circulation, Blood-tissue transport of solutes in the microcirculation and Membrane transport processes. Mass Transport in Biological Systems: Introduction to fundamental principles of mass transport and its application to biological systems, Microcirculation, Starling’s law, Rouleaux Effect, Segre–Silberberg effect, Fähraeus-Lindqvist effect and Fick's Law of Diffusion.
Module 3: Specialized Biological Transport Mechanisms: Gas and Solute Exchange, Pulmonary Gas Exchange, Alveolar Gas Equation and Transport pathways across the human Blood-brain barrier. Heat Transfer: Heat transfer in biological systems, Counter heat exchange and Bioheat Equation.
Module 4: Pharmacology and Drug Delivery: Pharmacokinetics: Drug distribution patterns and Drug Delivery Systems: Transdermal drug delivery system

Course Objective

1 .

To know the various fluid mechanics concepts and applications in biological process
2 .

To understand the transport phenomenon at the molecular, cellular, tissue, and organism level
3 .

To introduce the applicability of principles of heat and mass transfer in biological systems

Course Outcome

1 .

Gain the fundamental concepts of mass transfer, in the biological transport processes
Apply fluid mechanics principles to the solve problems in the bio-transport process
Gain knowledge in the transport process of liquid and gas in the biological system
Understand the applicability of heat transfer in the biological system
Familiarise with the basic concepts of drug pharmacokinetics

Essential Reading

1 .

A.T Jonhson, Biological Process Engineering, John Wiley, New York, 1999

2 .

C. G. Geankoplis, Transport Processes and Unit Operations, Allyn and Bacon, Boston, 1983

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Frank P. Incropera and David P. DeWitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, John Wiley & Sons 5th edition 2006

2 .

D. J. Haynie, Biological thermodynamics, Cambridge, 2008

19810.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE4709 : Steel Structures Design Practice { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Structural Steel Design Principles and IS 800:2007 Provisions: Introduction to limit state design philosophy, structural steel sections, material properties, loading standards, estimation of design loads, and design provisions as per IS 800:2007. (3 hours)
Module 2 :

Design and Detailing of Bolted and Welded Connections: Design and detailing of bolted and welded connections in a steel structure. (3 hours)
Module 3 :

Design of Tension Members: Design of tension members considering yielding, rupture, and block shear failure. (3 hours)
Module 4 :

Design of Compression Members: Design of steel compression members in a steel structure. (3 hours)
Module 5 :

Design of Column Bases and Anchor Bolts: Design of slab base, gusseted base, base plates, anchor bolts. (3 hours)
Module 6 :

Design of Beams, Purlins, and Beam-Columns: Design of beams, purlins, and beam-columns in a steel structure. (3 hours)
Module 7 :

Design of Plate Girders: Design of plate girders, including flange and web design, stiffeners, and checks for shear buckling and web crippling. (3 hours)
Module 8 :

Introduction to Structural Modelling and Analysis using Staad.Pro: Introduction to Staad.Pro interface, generation of structural geometry, assignment of material properties, supports, loading, and analysis procedures. (3 hours)
Module 9 :

Basic Steel Design Steps and Output Interpretation using Staad.Pro: Introduction to steel design workflow in Staad.Pro, design parameter assignment, interpretation of analysis and design outputs, and verification with hand calculations. (3 hours)
Module 10 :

Preparation of Structural Steel Drawings and Detailing: Preparation of structural steel drawings and detailing based on hand calculations and Staad.Pro outputs, including column layouts, framing plans, roofing plans, connection details, and base plate and anchor bolt detailing.(3 hours)

Course Objective

1 .

Provide hands-on experience in designing structural steel components and connections using design specifications and codes.
2 .

Enhance students’ ability to apply limit state design principles to real-world structural steel projects.
3 .

Develop problem-solving skills through practical design assignments.
4 .

Prepare students to integrate theoretical knowledge with practical applications in steel structure design.

Course Outcome

1 .

Apply IS 800:2007 provisions and estimate design loads for the analysis and design of steel structural systems.
2 .

Analyze steel structures and design tension and compression members using limit state design principles.
3 .

Design bolted and welded connections, column bases, and anchor bolts for steel structures using limit state design principles.
4 .

Design beams and beam-columns in steel structures using limit state design principles.
5 .

Prepare professional-quality design documentation that includes calculations, sketches, and design reports for real-world applications.

2 .

BIS, IS 800 (2007): Indian Standard General Construction in Steel - Code of Practice, Bureau of Indian Standards, New Delhi

2 .

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CR6437 : Refractories for Metallurgical and Allied Processes { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Review of metallurgical processes. Iron and steel making principles. Refractories used in Glass production, Cement industries, Lime calcinations, regenerators, Pottery industries and allied industries. Refractories for the refineries:- Duration - 6 h
Module 2 :

Refractories used in the coke oven, blast furnace, properties and problems. Refractories for hot metal handling. steel refining and secondary steel making. Ladle refractories, Direct bonded mag-chrome aggregates:- Duration - 6 h
Module 3 :

Continuous casting refractories: materials, production, properties and future trends. New generation slide gate refractories with improved performance. Hot repairing – Materials, repairing techniques :- Duration - 6 h
Module 4 :

Principles of extraction of non-ferrous metals of commercial importance especially Cu, Zn and Al. Types of furnaces and refractories used. Factors affecting the performance of refractories:- Duration - 6 h
Module 5 :

Refractories used for cement industries (different zones of preheater and rotary kiln), glass industries (mainly glass tank furnace, regenerator, etc), ceramic industries (refractory, whiteware, etc):- Duration - 6 h
Module 6 :

Standardisation, testing – including non–destructive testing. Plant trial performance of non-shaped and advanced refractories developed using surface chemistry, thermo-mechanical considerations for refractory linings. Use of non-oxide ceramic materials in ferrous and non-ferrous industries. Future trends in the utilisation of refractories. Recent advances in this area.- Duration - 6 h

Course Objective

1 .

To learn in details different high temperature metallurgical processes used commercially and industrially
2 .

To gain knowledge on the different types of refractories used for making iron, including coke oven, sinter plant and lime kiln
3 .

To know the different common and advanced refractories used for steel making and the continuous casting process
4 .

To learn the refractories that are used for different non-ferrous metallurgical industries, namely Al, Cu, etc.
5 .

To know the processes for making cement, glass and other non-metallurgical products and the details of the refractories used for making them
6 .

To learn in detail the standards of testing, refractory properties, testing methods as per the standards, etc

Course Outcome

1 .

Knowledge on different commercially used high temperature metallurgical processes
2 .

Knowledge of the refractories used in different kilns and furnaces for making iron
3 .

Knowledge on different conventional and advanced refractories used for steel making and casting
4 .

Knowledge on the refractories used for making Al, Cu, other non-ferrous metals
5 .

Knowledge on making cement, glass, etc non-metallurgical processes and the refractories used

Knowledge on different refractory properties, their standards, and standard testing methods

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Structural Principles [12 classes]: Crystal Systems, Unit cell, Bravias lattices, symmetry elements, Crystallographic point groups, representation of point groups, space groups and their representation. Types of close packing - hcp and ccp, packing efficiency, radius ratios polyhedral description of solids structure types -NaCl, ZnS, Na2O, CdCl2, wurtzite, nickel arsenide, CsCl, CdI2, rutile and Cs2O, perovskite ABO3, K2NiF4, spinels.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PH4009 : Electrodynamics { 3-1-0 / 4}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: (8 hours)
Green’s theorem, Method of Green’s function, Solution to boundary value problems using method of images and Green's functions technique, Green's reciprocation theorem, Green's Functions in Spherical Coordinates.
Module 2: (6 hours)
Poynting theorem and energy conservation by EM fields, Maxwell's stress tensor and momentum conservation with examples.
Module 3: (14 hours)
Electromagnetic (EM) waves in vacuum, Energy and momentum in EM waves, Boundary conditions for EM waves in matter, Reflection and transmission of EM waves, EM waves in conductors and dielectrics, Normal and anomalous dispersion, Causality and the Kramers-Kronig relations.
Module 4: (6 hours)
Waveguides, Boundary conditions, Rectangular and circular waveguides, TE, TM and TEM modes, Coaxial cables.
Module 5: (4 hours)
Potential formulation: Scalar and Vector Potential, Gauge invariance, Coulomb gauge and Lorentz gauge, Retarded potentials.
Module 6: (8 hours)
Electric field in different reference frames, Radiation from a point charge, Radiation from electric and magnetic dipoles, Radiation reaction, Radiation damping.

Course Objective

1 .

To learn the principles of electrodynamics and to apply Maxwell’s equations for calculating the electric and magnetic fields.
2 .

To learn to solve boundary value problems involving electric and magnetic fields.
3 .

To understand how energy and momenta are conserved by the EM fields.
4 .

To understand the principles of EM wave transmission through different media and waveguides.
5. To learn about the radiation from moving charges and oscillating dipoles.

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, students will be able to:
CO1: Write down the fundamental equations governing the behavior of EM fields in bulk and the boundary conditions at the interface.
CO2: Explain how energy and momenta are conserved by EM fields.
CO3: Apply those equations to characterize the propagation of EM waves through different types of media.
CO4: Apply Green’s function method to solve boundary value problems.
CO5: Examine the characteristics of EM radiation by point charges and dipoles.

Essential Reading

1 .

D. J. Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, Cambridge University Press , 4th Edition (2020).

2 .

A. Zangwill, Modern Electrodynamics, Cambridge University Press , 1st Edition (2012).

Supplementary Reading

1 .

J. D. Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, Wiley , 3rd Edition (2007).

2 .

D. J. Morin and E. M. Purcell, Electricity and Magnetism, Cambridge University Press , 3rd Edition (2013).

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ER5247 : Rheology of the Earth { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Fundamentals of Earth’s Rheology - Introduction to crustal deformation: stress, strain, and rheology of Earth's lithosphere Elastic, viscous, and plastic behavior of geological materials Lithospheric rheology: brittle, ductile, and viscoelastic deformation Experimental and theoretical approaches in rheological studies.
Module 2: Rock Deformation Mechanisms - Frictional sliding and fracture mechanics in brittle materials Crystal plasticity: diffusion creep, dislocation creep, and grain boundary sliding High-pressure and high-temperature rock deformation experiments Influence of temperature, pressure, and fluid presence on rock rheology.
Module 3: Volcanic Deformation and Eruption Dynamics - Strength profiles of the continental and oceanic lithosphere Mantle convection and viscoelastic relaxation Geodynamic processes: isostatic adjustment, post-glacial rebound, and plate motions Seismic anisotropy and deformation in the asthenosphere.
Module 4: Rheology and Tectonic Processes - Rheology of faults and subduction zones: implications for earthquake cycles Strain localization in the lithosphere: shear zones and fault weakening mechanisms Crust-mantle interactions: lithospheric flexure and mountain building The role of fluids in controlling deformation and seismicity.
Module 5: Rheological Modeling and Applications - Analytical and numerical modeling of lithospheric and mantle rheology Maxwell, Kelvin-Voigt, and Burgers models for Earth materials Applications in geodynamic modeling: mantle plumes, rift dynamics, and crustal deformation: Case studies: post-seismic relaxation, glacial isostatic adjustment, and subduction zone rheology.

Course Objective

1 .

Understanding the Rheological Properties of Earth Materials – Introduce fundamental concepts of stress-strain relationships, deformation mechanisms, and rheological behaviors in geological materials.
2 .

Exploring Deformation Mechanisms in the Lithosphere and Mantle – Examine brittle, ductile, and viscoelastic deformation in Earth's lithosphere and deeper mantle.
3 .

Analyzing the Role of Rheology in Geodynamic and Tectonic Processes – Investigate the implications of rheology on fault mechanics, mountain building, and mantle convection.
4 .

Applying Rheological Models in Earth Sciences – Develop and apply analytical and numerical models to study crustal and mantle rheology.
Integrating Rheology into Seismic and Geodynamic Studies – Use rheological principles to interpret seismic anisotropy, post-glacial rebound, and long-term Earth deformation.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. To understand fundamental rheological principles and their application in Earth sciences.
2. To analyze deformation mechanisms in rocks at different pressure-temperature conditions.
3. To evaluate lithospheric and mantle rheology using experimental and observational data.
4. To apply rheological models for geodynamic and tectonic process simulations.
5. To integrate rheological knowledge into seismic hazard assessment and geodynamic studies.

Essential Reading

1 .

Shun-Ichiro Karato, Deformation of Earth Materials, Cambridge University press , 2008

2 .

G. Ranalli, The Rheology of Earth, Cambridge University press , 1998

Supplementary Reading

1 .

J. Jaeger, N. G. Cook and R. Zimmerman, Fundamentals of Rock Mechanics, Wiley-Blackwell , 4th edition, 2007

2 .

Paul Segall, Earthquake and Volcano deformation, Princeton press , 2002

Module 1 :

Module I
Study principles and methods of construction of R.C.C. structure: Beams including cantilever beams, columns, slabs including one-way, two-way and cantilever slabs, roof including vaults and domes form-work techniques and reinforcement details.
Module II
Foundations: Study of principles and methods of construction of R.C.C. foundations and columns types of foundations – raft foundations, grillage foundations and combination pile foundation – precast piles, cast-in-situ piles, types of piles, method of driving piles, pile caps etc.
Module III
Shoring and its types underpinning scaffolding and its types.
Module IV
Expansion joints: Construction details at foundation, walls, floors and roof level for concrete and brickwork.
Module V
Construction of upper floors: General considerations flag stone floor on steel joist concrete jack arch floor reinforced cement concrete floor including flat slab construction, ribbed floor and precast concrete floor. Construction, R.C.C. staircase.
Module VI
Waterproofing at the flat roof Damp proofing at the basement.
Module VII
Plaster: Method of plastering internal plaster (use of various finishes viz., lime, cement, plaster of Paris) external plaster (smooth, rough, textured, grit plaster) cladding – types and method of construction

Course Objective

1 .

To familiarize students with the construction method and techniques adopted for various stages of reinforced concrete construction.
2 .

To interpret and produce the actual drawing requirements and the various aspects of drawings for the reinforced concrete construction.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Ability to familiarize the students with the construction method and techniques adopted for various stages of project execution on site.
2. Ability to develop and learn the actual drawing requirements and the various aspects of drawing for reinforced concrete construction.
